claims.text: Increasing the Pd fraction in a NiFeCoCr-based high-entropy alloy will increase its coercive field.
Pd addition will boost magnetic anisotropy.
Pd addition produces stronger spin-orbit coupling in the alloy.
Pd addition makes the distribution of exchange interactions more uniform.
NiFeCoCr with low or no Pd has a broader distribution of exchange energies than Pd-containing variants.
Integrating Pd atoms into NiFeCoCr enhances lattice distortion.
The Pd-induced lattice and spin-orbit effects increase magnetic anisotropy.
Pd is heavier than the constituent elements of the baseline NiFeCoCr alloy.
Enhanced spin-orbit coupling caused by Pd makes exchange interactions more uniform.
Greater magnetic anisotropy, more uniform exchange interactions, and increased domain-wall pinning collectively raise coercivity.
The coercivity enhancement should hold when processing and heat treatment preserve a single-phase, microstructurally homogeneous alloy.
The coercivity enhancement is limited to a compositional range in which the alloy remains single-phase and microstructurally stable.
Excessive Pd may cause phase separation or other deleterious changes that negate the coercivity benefit.
Pd additions reduce the exchange-energy distribution and make NiFeCoCrPdx magnetically more homogeneous.
A lack of a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to the matched no-Pd baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis only predicts an increase over baseline within a stable compositional range, but the falsification rule additionally requires observation of an optimal Pd level before deleterious effects appear. A monotonic increase up to the phase-stability boundary could support the stated hypothesis while still satisfying this extra falsification condition.
